newsitem.title: HAITI: Disillusioned Haitians stay away from polls.
newsitem.headline: Disillusioned Haitians stay away from polls.

text.p: Disillusioned, frustrated and hungrier by the day, Haitians stayed away in droves from senate and local elections on Sunday in what appeared to be a silent protest against the government.

In the decrepit downtown of Port-au-Prince, crammed slum of Cite Soleil, and southern coast town of Jacmel, election officials stood by exasperated in the morning as individuals wandered by every so often to cast ballots.
While it was likely that voting would pick-up after Sunday mass finished, many people gathered outside polling stations in Port-au-Prince said they did not plan to cast a ballot.
They said they had felt let down by politicians and dismayed by government privatisation plans which would only make life harder in an already desperately poor country.

"We are hungry. We can't vote for millionaires. The senators got millions from the Americans and what did we get? Nothing. If they pay us we'll vote," said one man outside the Alexandre Petain school in Port-au-Prince as a crowd shouted its agreement.
President Rene Preval voted in mid-morning in the capital, telling reporters: "This is an important moment. It expresses the will of the nation."
Election officials said he was the first person to vote there other than themselves. No one was waiting behind him.

The polls are the fifth electoral exercise in Haiti since a U.S. military intervention ousted a military regime and restored the popular president Jean-Bertand Aristide to power in October 1994. Preval was elected as his successor in December 1995.

But Preval's plans to ease poverty through a privatisation programme backed with huge infusions of international aid have stalled. Discontent is simmering with little evidence of anything tangible being done to lift the people out of their misery.
Unemployment is more than 70 percent and the average income is $250 a year. Social services are virtually non-existant and the country's infrastructure is in ruins.

"The country is in a bad situation. They voted for candidates and when they came into power candidates voted for privatisation laws. We are in a situation where people don't believe anymore," said Lebrun Ruoat, chief electoral supervisor at the school, where poll officials outnumbered voters.
More than four million Haitains are registered to vote. At stake are nine seats in the 27-seat Senate, two parliamentary seats, 133 town delegations and 565 district assemblies.

The elections aim to bring democratic rule to a local level for the first time in the history of the Caribbean state, which gained independence from France with a slave revolt in 1804 but has since suffered a tortured history of rule by dictators and generals, sometimes supported and other times opposed by the United States.

Foreign analysts say the poll will signal what the future may hold for Haiti. The ruling Lavalas Political Organisation has already split over privatisation. Aristide founded the Famni Lavalas (Lavalas Family) in November and it is fielding slates of candidates against former colleagues.
Senator Yvon Neptune said Famni Lavalas carried the banner of the party of the poor.

"Famni Lavalas is against the exploitation of the Haitian people and against decisions supposedly taken in their name but without them having a say in it," he said, referring to the international community's plans for Haiti.
